title: Hands
subtitle: Sherwood Anderson (1919) — a lonely man in a small Ohio town, a pair of restless hands, and the rumour that made them.
crosslink: Need an easier version? Read this story at A2/B1 level →
grammar_tab: Grammar — The Passive: What Was Done to Him
intention: you'll tell the story of a man destroyed by a rumour, and use the passive — was driven out, had been beaten, is talked about — for what is done to a person by people who are never named.
warmup: Think of a small town or a village you know. How fast does a rumour travel there — and does it ever go away?
What do people's hands tell you about them? Think of someone whose hands you remember.
A teacher is accused of something by a child. What should happen first — and what usually happens?
vocab_intro: Before we read, let's unlock the words you'll need. Think first — the Reveal only confirms.

vocab.heading: A. Work it out from the sentence
vocab.instruction: Read each sentence aloud and say what the bold word means from the rest of the sentence. Then reveal.

items.sent: For twenty years he had been beset by doubts: every look in the street, every silence, seemed to accuse him of something.
items.meaning: beset (adj / v, usually passive) — surrounded and troubled by problems or fears on all sides.

items.sent: The question had been in his mind for months, and one evening he nearly blurted it out before he could stop himself.
items.meaning: to blurt out (phrasal v) — to say something suddenly and without thinking.

items.sent: The old man hurried away without a word, leaving the boy perplexed on the hillside — what had he done wrong?
items.meaning: perplexed (adj) — confused and worried because you cannot understand something.

items.sent: They let him go — then, ashamed of their kindness, they repented of it and ran after him with sticks.
items.meaning: to repent of (v) — to feel regret for something you have done; here, ironically, for a moment of mercy.

vocab.heading: B. Build the word
vocab.instruction: You know one form of the word. Say the form the sentence needs, then reveal.

items.sent: You know timid. In the boy's presence he 'lost something of his ___' — what is the noun?
You know devote (to give yourself to something). What is the noun for a person who does this — a religious ___?
items.meaning: a devotee (n) — a person deeply devoted to a religion, a practice or an activity. devote → devotee

items.sent: The French word for love is amour. What English adjective, with 'en-' in front, means 'in love with, infatuated'?
items.meaning: enamoured (adj) — in love with; filled with admiration. became enamoured of the young master (American spelling: enamored)

vocab.heading: C. Choose the meaning
vocab.instruction: One sentence, three options. Say a, b or c — then reveal.

items.sent: The hands made more grotesque an already strange and elusive personality. Grotesque means: (a) strong and healthy (b) ugly or distorted in a way that is disturbing, almost comic (c) famous
items.meaning: (b) — grotesque (adj) — strangely distorted, ugly or absurd. Anderson called the people of Winesburg his 'grotesques'.

items.sent: He raised the hands to caress the boy's shoulders. To caress is: (a) to touch gently and lovingly (b) to push away (c) to hold tightly
items.meaning: (a) — to caress (v) — to touch or stroke gently, with affection. Also a noun: a caress.

items.sent: Hidden doubts about the teacher were galvanised into beliefs. To galvanise is: (a) to calm down (b) to forget (c) to shock into sudden action or certainty
items.meaning: (c) — to galvanise (v) — to shock or excite into sudden action; here, to turn vague suspicion into hard certainty.

vocab_use: Put the ten words in the order you'd expect them in a story about a shy man and a town that turns on him. Say why.
Using beset, caress and galvanise, predict what the man's hands have to do with his fear.
story_intro: Anderson's own text, lightly shortened. This is the first story in Winesburg, Ohio. Read each part; after it, try the quick check from memory, then talk about the question.

story.title: Part 1 — The man on the veranda

skip: A boy clad in a blue shirt

check.q: Who is the one person in Winesburg who has come close to Wing Biddlebaum, and what happens to Wing when that person is with him?
check.a: George Willard, the young reporter. In his presence Wing loses his timidity: his low trembling voice becomes loud, his bent figure straightens, and he talks excitedly, 'like a fish returned to the brook'.

check.q: How does Wing feel about his own hands?
check.a: They alarm him. He tries to hide them in his pockets or behind his back, and looks with amazement at other men's quiet hands; when he talks he beats his fists on a table or a fence to feel more comfortable.

story.discuss: Anderson tells us the hands gave Wing his name 'like the beating of the wings of an imprisoned bird'. What is imprisoned, and what is trying to get out?

story.title: Part 2 — 'I'll not ask him about his hands'

paras.from: The story of Wing Biddlebaum’s hands is worth a book
paras.to: fear of me and of everyone.”
skip: Winesburg was proud of the hands
On the grassy bank Wing Biddlebaum had tried again

check.q: What does Wing tell George he must do — and what does he do with his hands as he says it?
check.a: That George must stop imitating the people around him, forget what he has learned, dream, and 'shut his ears to the roaring of the voices'. For once he forgets the hands, and they steal out and rest on George's shoulders.

check.q: Why does Wing suddenly run away, and what does George decide?
check.a: A look of horror crosses his face when he raises his hands to touch the boy again; he thrusts them into his pockets and hurries home in tears. George decides never to ask about the hands — 'there's something wrong, but I don't want to know what it is'.

story.discuss: Wing's advice to George — stop copying the town, dare to dream — is the best advice in the story. Why does it come from the man the town despises?

story.title: Part 3 — Adolph Myers

paras.to: decade after decade of his rosary.
skip: Perhaps our talking of them will arouse
In their feeling for the boys under
He was one of those men in whom the force
As his hard knuckles beat down
He had an aunt in Winesburg
Going into his house he cut slices

check.q: Who was Adolph Myers, and what exactly started the 'tragedy'?
check.a: A young schoolteacher in Pennsylvania, loved by his pupils, who touched their shoulders and hair as he talked. A 'half-witted' boy who had become enamoured of him told his night-time dreams as facts, and the town's hidden doubts hardened into belief.

check.q: What did the town do to him, and how did he come to be called Wing Biddlebaum?
check.a: The saloon keeper beat him in the schoolyard; a dozen men came at night with lanterns and a rope, meant to hang him, let him run, then chased him with sticks and mud. He took the name Biddlebaum from a box at a freight station as he fled, and lived twenty years in Winesburg, hiding his hands, sure they were to blame.

story.discuss: Anderson never says outright that Adolph Myers was innocent; he says the accusations were dreams told as facts, and that Myers 'did not understand what had happened'. Does the story convince you? Should it have said more — or less?

grammar.h2: The grammar this story runs on: the passive — what was done to him
grammar.intro: Nobody in this story is named as responsible. Boys 'were jerked out of bed'; a man 'was driven from the town'; doubts 'were galvanised into beliefs'. The passive lets a writer show what happened to a person while the people who did it stay in the shadows — which is exactly Anderson's point.
notes:
1. Form: be + past participle, in any tense.
• past simple: "The shop was closed by the council." • past continuous: "The bridge was being repaired."
• past perfect: "By dawn the letters had been burnt." • present perfect: "She has been offered the job."
• with modals: "He could be seen from the road."

2. Leaving out the agent. Use by + agent only when it matters. "He was beaten" (we don't say by whom — or everyone knows, or nobody will admit it). This is the passive's great power in a story about a town.

3. Two extras.
• get-passive, informal, for things that happen to people: "He got beaten up." "She got promoted."
• Passive with prepositional verbs — keep the preposition: "His hands are talked about." "The boy was laughed at." "He was looked after by an aunt."

exercises.h3: Put the verb in the passive, in the tense the hint gives
exercises.instruction: Read each one aloud when you've filled it. Notice how no one is named.
items: Adolph Myers ___ (drive) out of the Pennsylvania town in the night. (past simple)
Trembling boys ___ (jerk) out of bed and ___ (question). (past simple, twice)
For twenty years he ___ (know) as the town mystery. (past perfect)
The hands ___ (name) by some obscure poet of the town. (past simple)
He ___ (never / understand) — not even by himself. (past simple)

exercises.h3: Turn it round — and drop the agent
exercises.instruction: Rewrite in the passive without saying who did it. The tense stays the same.
items: A dozen men drove him from the town. → He ___ from the town.
The saloon keeper beat him in the schoolyard. → He ___ in the schoolyard.
People in Winesburg talk about his hands. → His hands ___ in Winesburg.
Somebody had given him the name Wing. → He ___ the name Wing.
The town's doubts have never quite left him. → He ___ by the town's doubts. (use: haunt)
answers: has been haunted (has never quite been left alone — but has been haunted is the natural one)

exercises.h3: Put it together — twenty years in one paragraph
exercises.instruction: Fill each gap with the passive form the hint asks for. Read it aloud when you've finished.
items: Adolph Myers ___ (love / past simple) by the boys of his school. Then one boy's dreams ___ (tell / past simple) as facts, old doubts ___ (galvanise / past simple) into beliefs, and within a week the teacher ___ (beat / past perfect) in his own schoolyard and ___ (chase / past perfect) into the dark with sticks and mud. In Winesburg his hands ___ (admire / present simple) and he himself ___ (leave alone / present simple).
answers: was loved · were told · were galvanised · had been beaten · had been chased · are admired · is left alone
exercises.note: Count the agents: none. That is how a whole town escapes responsibility in one paragraph.

grammar.outro: In the Speak tab, tell what was done to Wing in the passive — and then decide whether you want to name the agents.

deeper.h2: Why this story stays with you
paras: Sherwood Anderson (1876–1941) was a paint-company manager in Ohio who walked out of his office one day in 1912 and became a writer. Winesburg, Ohio (1919), twenty-two linked stories about the buried lives of one small town, changed American fiction: Hemingway and Faulkner both learned from it. 'Hands' is its first story, and Anderson said he wrote it in one sitting and never changed a word.

The story is built on a gap. Anderson tells us the accusations were a disturbed boy's dreams 'told as facts', that Myers 'did not understand what had happened', that the hands were only 'fluttering pennants of promise' — and then, twice, he says the truth of the matter 'needs the poet' and refuses to say it. What is certain is what the town did with its certainty: a beating, a rope, twenty years of silence. The last image — a kneeling man picking crumbs from the floor 'like a priest' with a rosary — turns the hands the town feared into something holy, and leaves it to us to decide whether that is consolation or the cruellest thing in the story.
deeper.note: Look again at the town's pride. Winesburg is 'proud of the hands of Wing Biddlebaum' because they pick a hundred and forty quarts of strawberries a day — 'in the same spirit' as it is proud of a banker's stone house and a fast horse. What is Anderson saying about how a town values a person?
questions: Wing tells George: 'You want to be like others in town here… you try to imitate them.' Is the story about one man's tragedy, or about what a town does to anyone who is different?
George decides not to ask. Is his silence kindness, cowardice, or the same thing the town did — refusing to know?
The men came with a rope, felt pity, let him run, and then were ashamed of their pity. Anderson calls the pity 'weakness'. Is he being ironic? Do crowds really repent of mercy?
In 1919 Anderson could not say plainly what the town suspected. Read the story today: does its refusal to be explicit make it more honest about how rumour works, or less?

speak.useful: The passive for what happened to him: "He was driven out…", "He had been beaten…", "His hands are talked about…". When you decide to name the agents: "by a saloon keeper", "by a dozen men with lanterns". For opinions: "What's striking is…", "You could argue that…", "The story refuses to say whether…".

tasks.label: Task A · Tell the whole story (4 minutes)
paras: Tell 'Hands' to someone who has never read it. Move through the arc: the nervous man on the veranda → George Willard, the one friend → the hands and the town's pride → the afternoon on the hillside → Adolph Myers the teacher → the boy's dreams, the beating, the rope → twenty years in Winesburg → the crumbs and the rosary.
Use the passive deliberately for what was done to him, and at least five key words (beset, blurt out, perplexed, repent, timidity, devotee, enamoured, grotesque, caress, galvanise).

tasks.label: Task B · The town's defence (4 minutes)
paras: Take the town's side: a child made an accusation, other boys confirmed it, the fathers acted to protect their sons. Make the strongest possible case that they did what any parents would do. Then switch sides and answer it — what did the town fail to do, and what did it want to believe?

tasks.label: Task C · Driven out (4 minutes)
paras: Tell a story — real, famous or invented — about a person who was pushed out by rumour, suspicion or a mistaken accusation, and what became of them. Use the passive for what was done to them, and decide at the end whether to name who did it.
menu: A witch trial, in Salem or anywhere else, where the accusers were children.
A teacher, a doctor or a priest whose career was ended by an accusation later shown to be false.
A footballer or a politician 'cancelled' on social media within a day — rightly or wrongly.
A family in a village that everyone stopped speaking to, and nobody could quite say why.
A newcomer to a small town who never became 'one of us'.
Someone you have read about who changed their name and started again.

final: Anderson makes the hands holy at the end — a priest, a rosary. Is that what the story earns, or is it Anderson refusing to face what he has written?
Twenty years later, Wing still believes 'the hands must be to blame'. What does it do to a person to accept the town's verdict on themselves?
Is there anyone in your world who is 'talked about' the way Wing is? What would it take to ask them?
Before you go — from memory: give me three things that were done to Adolph Myers, in the passive, in three different tenses — and then say who did them.
